correctness.rationale: Gaussian Fourier differentiation in degrees four and two forces the quadratic part to be −ΔQ/(8π), cancels the constant transform correction exactly, and rules out Q≡0 for a nonzero eigenfunction with f(0)=0. If A=Q|_S is negative anywhere, it is uniformly negative on a smaller spherical patch and the leading term forces an infinite-volume negative cone at large radii. If A>0, the directional squared endpoint is u=((d+2)/(2π)+Δ_SA/(8πA))_+ (the later ν notation refers to the same untruncated expression defined as u in line 66). Exact polar integration and convexity of the positive-part d/2 power give the claimed inequality because spherical integration by parts gives E[Δ_SA/A]=E|∇_S log A|². This average is strictly positive unless A is constant. For nonnegative A with zeros, the perturbation Q+ε|x|⁴ changes f by εe^(−πr²)r²(r²−R₀²). Inside R₀, volume convergence follows by dominated convergence on a finite-volume ball and the null polynomial zero set; outside R₀, indicators for the strict negative set increase to the original indicator as ε decreases. A nonconstant nonnegative smooth A has a patch with A>0 and gradient bounded away from zero, producing a uniform positive angular penalty for the perturbations. Thus the limit is strictly above the radial minimum, including if it is infinite. Direct polar integration of the planar harmonic perturbation gives 2/√(1−ε²); independently computed angular quadrature at ε=0.2 and 0.8 corroborated the areas 2.0412414523 and 3.3333333333 and saturation of the planar angular bound. The nested artifacts/verify_quartic.py was inspected but not executed. Its recorded sample calculations are not a proof of the full-shell theorem.
